strTitle: View News on Strange Watch Parties
strDesc: [us] [watches] [them] more closely and learn about a group of eccentrics who gather in secret to watch what they describe as rare and mind altering video footage. The segment B-roll shows a makeshift theater on Flotilla full of viewers with blurred faces watching the footage and smoking from large shared pipes.
[us] tries scouring local and social media sources using [them] for info about the drug fueled watch parties around OKLG.

[them] [uses] [them] to find a constellation of cryptic forum posts that make reference to The Flotilla, gold, something called The Black Sun, and a strange video format you have never heard of called a VHS tape.

It's a small black obelisk, unlike anything you've ever seen before.

You wave your PDA at it and wait for the image recognition suite to resolve. It's a 'videotape', says the precis, a kind of early analogue storage medium accessed via a VHS player. It eagerly regurgitates guff about the Format Wars. You swipe it away.

The shell has two clear windows on the front. Through those there are two spools holding a reel of tape. Maybe it's like a laundry back on the station, and you can look inside the player and watch the tape running.

What the hell was it doing out here?
strTooltip: Give the box a closer look

strDesc:
You turn the shell over in your hands. The reverse side is covered with colourful stickers.

<mark=#ffd700ff><color="black">               BE KIND, REWIND :)<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>

<mark=#ff0000ff><color="black">               WARNING: DO NOT COPY.<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>
<mark=#ff0000ff><color="black">               COPYING TAPES IS A FELONY<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>

<mark=#ff00ffff><color="green">               NEW RELEASE! ONE NIGHT RENTAL!<alpha=#00>a</alpha></color></mark>

The PDA seems to think they are era-appropriate, which does not help you.

You notice one of the long edges has bright orange tape stuck to it. Thick block letters written with a marker pen read, <mark=#ffa600ff><color="black">    "VOID OPAL INHALANTS #3."     </color></mark> This one, which must be its title, makes even less sense.

Maybe you need to see Inhalants 1 & 2 to get it.

There's no use staring at the tape. The two unblinking windows in its hull aren't going to budge. You've got to ask other people about it, and it's not like you've got any friends - any who know about legacy home media, that is. Why not see what the local station net has to say?
strTooltip: The internet will know what to do

strDesc: The PDA glows, ready to assist you with your search.

strTitle: Hunt for any discussions of videotapes
strDesc: K-LEG has three main bulletin boards: the Ayotimiwa employee forums, the K-LEG official Subreddit, and Cho-Cho-Cho, the latter of which is by far the most popular, even if most of the features don't work. It's built that way on purpose. A cursory scan of the employee forums turns up nothing, and the subreddit has only a sticky post about how it's evil to pirate media. CCC, on the other hand, has more to say. You read several long chat threads about a 'videotape' and how excited the posters are to see it live. These actually concern an X-pop singer whose new single, videotape, is charting well across the inner system. But soon enough you strike gold. It's a locked thread, and the OP's account has been deleted. What remains are the replies from another concerned user, leaving behind a one sided conversation. >>> Do you mean like box? How big > DELETED >>> Ohh, I get you. no never. But ill keep my eyes peeled. > DELETED >>> Sorry i misunderstood. Sure I can take a look at it. Im at NoodlEgg stand for another 15 if you want to meet. > DELETED >>> hello? :fish_emoji: The timestamps are ten minutes apart between the final few posts. It's unclear if the deleted user showed up.

The K-LEG Q/A boards are awash with a Brownian motion of boredom and moderator tyranny. The top three pages are complaints about questions that have been answered a million times, shoulder to shoulder with posts asking those same evergreen questions.
Trying to view the half-deleted thread throws 404 errors. It's as if that page never existed at all.

Maybe you need to keep it circumspect. You catch more flies with honey. "Has anyone seen Void Inhalants #3?" is the title and body of your post. There's a flurry of engagement. No text, just thumbs down. You pick a fingernail as you wait, listening to the swish and hum of an A/C unit. Finally there's a hit. "Hello! Not 3, but I've seen 2, 7, and 8," says the reply. The avatar is a big upside down smiling face, a match for their handle - 'Smiley'. "Do you have 3? What's in it?" "I was hoping you could help me with that," you tap back. "I don't know how it works." "We absolutely can," comes an instant reply. Who's we, all of a sudden? "You're K-LEG local, right? Come to Flotilla." Smiley attaches a string of numbers. Your PDA helpfully highlights it as a Flotilla residential address. "Any time! Day or night."
strSetPlotObjective: name|The Videotape: Find 'Smiley'|ct|CTPLOT_Ceres_Is_Smiley|desc|The person known as Smiley wants to meet you on Flotilla (OKLG_FLOT).

strTitle: Leave a plain description and request info
strDesc:
You jot down basic specs about the video tape, the size, shape, the cursory knowledge you've gained about VHS media, and ask the gen public if they've ever come across such a thing.

All that's left to do is wait for a kind internet stranger to - 

- hold on.

Your post vanishes before your eyes. Refreshing dumps you back to the CCC landing page. What the hell?

You scroll through catalogues and trade publications of Renbao et al, hoping to come across a niche division or indie outfit producing century-old home media. No dice. As far as the consumer electronics market is concerned, you cannot buy a tape nor player.

An automated sales rep from Renbao opens up a message window and prattles an offer for a bespoke rush manufacturing job to make your own replica VHS device. After a brief Q/A, it admits it has no idea what you (and it) are talking about.

"Can I speak to a human?" you type back.

"We don't have any humans here," it says. Apologetically, perhaps.
You pocket the tape and move on.
strSetPlotObjective: name|The Videotape: Research 'VHS'|ct|TIsPDAHeldUnlocked|desc|Return to an OKLG station and search the local mesh on your PDA.|img|ItmWristPDA01

strDesc:
In the way that a steel pipe pinwheeling forever through an airless cargo bay does not, this feels important.

There has to be an expert on K-LEG who knows more about this ... 'VHS'. Certainly not anyone you know, but someone on the station must.

You could try looking it up on OKLG's local internet. Your PDA can access it, provided you're on one of its affiliate stations.

You push through the heavy fabric that many dorms use to segregate their HVAC.

Inside is a wide common room with a low ceiling. Underfoot is a haphazard array of futons and padded flooring, all oriented toward a wall screen. There's a kitchenette in back. Smiley waits for you crosslegged on a futon, halo of hair gently settling around his shoulders. You take a seat opposite him.

"Show me," he says.

You produce the videotape. His eyes light up. "Hot damn!" he whoops. You let him yank it from your hands.

"This is the real deal," he says, poring over it, testing a sticker's binding agent with pinched fingers. "Like I told you, we've got a bunch of others, a 2, a 7, and a handful of 8s. Our first 3!"

You clear your throat. He refocuses on you, eyes blinking behind his enormous glasses.

"Right, right. What is it? It's a video. What's on the video? Freaky shit, man, freaky shit. People doing some kinda ritual. Who am I? Nobody. Who are we? We are, y'know, whoever wants to watch. We get together and we watch them. Compare notes, theorise. Argue. It's like a little club. Get me?"

You nod, considering it. "A ritual?"

He waves dismissively. "I'll show you, if you want. Don't fret. This is a huge day for us. It's been ages since we've had something new. I'm entirely at your disposal."

The man has a high forehead and a receding hairline. His hair, where it's growing, is long, reaching past his shoulders. He should be old, but his unblemished skin doesn't put him past thirty. He wears large trifocal glasses, and a wide, placid smile.

"Are you Smiley?" you ask. "From the message thread."

"Namaste," he says, "and jeete raho. I am he."

You murmur noncommittally. "I have the videotape. Do you know what it is? What it does?"

His smile grows wider. "It plays videos. Or it should, but if it's like the others, it's broken."

"But you've watched them."

"I have watched them."

"How?" You keep a lid on your impatience.

Smiley looks up and down the accessway conspiratorially. There's the average amount of people around for a Flotilla accessway, which is to say some, and an average amount of interest in your conversation, which is to say none. "Not here. Inside." Smiley vanishes into a residence.
strTooltip: He's waiting where he said he would be.

strDesc:
Smiley never really loses his trademark dopey smile, but it dims and brightens, and it brightens now. "I was hoping you would."

He queues up the video on the wall screen. The playback pauses tantalisingly on the first frame, twin bars of the pause symbol blocking the view. Smiley insists on first making a batch of his special popcorn, 'like how the food carts do it but better'.

While he hums from the kitchenette, you study the still frame.

It's a study in harsh light; the camera and subject are EVA. The top half of the frame is the dark side of an asteroid. The gentle curve of a horizon, where the black body becomes a curtain of stars, suggests it's a small rock, a hundred metres across, if that. A muted pop from behind you announces the first kernel's expansion.

Beneath the asteroid, hanging motionless (the video being paused) is the harsh silhouette of a spacesuit. Their arm is outstretched, gesturing up toward the surface like Adam reaching out to God.

The picture is grainy, pockmarked by imperfection. It could be due to the ISO of whatever this was captured on, but Smiley said this, here, was taken from a cellulose tape like the one you have ... so who knows when the imperfections were introduced?

Smiley suddenly reappears beside you, making you start. He waggles a bowl of popcorn. "Ready?" he says. "First time through, I won't say a thing. Then if you like, we can watch again and I can give you the Extras commentary track." 

He offers you the bowl.

"No can do," he says. He indicates your tape. "It's a dud. There's video in there, somewhere. But the first thing we did - this is going back - Abacho and Xavier kitbashed a working VHS player. We had to reverse engineer a head, this little needle thing to read the tape, and order it from a fab on Venus, and then we had to hound down some weirdo on Luna who insisted he had real copies of the PAL and NTSC video standards, and then he ghosted us, blah blah blah. That's kind of how the group got started." "And?" "And, long story short, we made a working VHS player. We think. It worked with some other tape we found at auction. But our damned tape wouldn't play. Know why?" There's no way you could know, but he's enjoying telling the story and he doesn't wait for you to answer. "Because it's a fake! It's not a VHS tape. It's a plastic replica holding a spool of modern, analog, cellulose film. Venus stock, where the cellulose comes from. We had never actually opened the damn thing to check." You have an obvious question coming, but it's been bugging you for a while, so you just come out with it. "Why would someone make this?" "We don't know! That's why it's so fascinating! We're running a pool." He brings up a spreadsheet on the wall screen. "Xavier has 300 on an ARG. Molly Liu thinks it's outsider art. Molly 2 thinks it's aliens. Xavier thinks," he rolls his eyes, "it's final proof that the universe is a simulation that's beginning to unravel. We don't like him very much but he put down a lot of cash, so whatever."

The video plays.

The motionless figure comes to life. At the apex of its arm's reach, a gas jet flares from its wrist. A flicker across the dark suggests a projectile fired up into the asteroid with a long trailing cable. The cable snaps taut, and the spacesuit flies up into the asteroid's penumbra. 

An enormous spacesuit helmet slides in front of the camera as a second figure enters the scene, the faceplate a brilliant reflection of the starry night, evoking that silent terror unique to a spacewalk. It drifts past the camera, offering a brief thumbs up, then fires its own grapple after the first suit.

As the second spacesuit travels, up becomes down, and it's falling. The camera's POV shifts to one side, and the tape abruptly has a -

Cut: 

Inserts flash past too quick to properly read. An alphanumeric string '1-400', a litany of memtest logs, the Voltaire university logo, which segues into a chintzy orientation video ripped straight from the interplanetary net. Audio snaps on, too loud after the silence, playing over Lunar students relaxing in a campus dorm. "- over ten thousand future fellows per intake, you're bound to find a loopmate for life." Students play a friendly scrimmage game of Breakout in a refectory hall. "That's how BNW is securing the future of our System, today."

Students pose in the iconic Voltaire quadrangle, laughing. The camera pulls back past the BNW CEO. He turns to camera, smiling. "Are You Prepared For Tomorrow?"

It seizes on -orrow, -orrow, -orrow, then turns dark and silent. 

Cut: 

A thin stripe of light cuts across the screen, revealing a rock fissure. The torch shines briefly back to the camera, a halo eating everything. It shines away. Its wielder is inching gingerly through the gap in the rock. Judging by the motion of the camera, so is the person filming.

Cut:

A black star. A black sun. The universe around it cast in white. Like a photo negative, or infrared. Its surface roils. Is it Sol? Can't say. Audio builds, an intermittent digital staccato repeating faster and faster until it becomes a voice, and then a cacophonous scream.

Cut:

"O Brave New World," says the CEO, reading from a teleprompter, "that has such people in it." He gestures to his flock of happy undergrads.

"Cut!" someone calls. The undergrads dissolve into a backlit white wall. The CEO wilts against the blank LED volume. "We got it," another voice says reassuringly.

"Thank fucking God," he says, turning offscreen. "I get to the very end - tell marketing to give me simple sentences -"

Cut:

Torches play over another unlit cavern of the asteroid. One of the two spacesuits comes over to the camera's POV. Arms reach out. The POV shifts and settles. Violently? No. It's framing. The spacesuit drifts away.

Overhead lights snap on, bright and powerful. A small prefab room, barely more than a sealed plastic bubble expanded into the rock wall.

In the centre of the chamber, something enormous glitters. An effigy, humanoid, long. A bulbous head. Arms crossed over its torso. Detailed engravings give it the semblance of a slumbering human. An effigy? No, a sarcophagus.

It is made of perfect gold.

The media player reaches the end of the track.

"How," you say, accessing a well of patience you never knew you possessed, "do we see what's on my tape, then?" "Easy," says Smiley. "There's a woman here on Flotilla, she digitises them for us. Isambard Cruz. Take it to her, tell her I sent you. Or don't. I don't think she likes me very much." "That sucks," you say neutrally. "In any case, you'll have to call her on her intercom. You'll find it on the door, right down the hall here." Smiley continues. "She, uh. Doesn't get out much." He gives you the intercom door location on Flotilla, down the hall and one turn away. "And can you promise to bring back a copy to us? Finders keepers, salvage rights, et cetera. But," he says apologetically, "I've already organised a watch party, tonight. Everyone's losing their mind, dying to see a new tape. Would you come? You'd be the hero of the hour." "I'll see what I can do."
strSetPlotObjective: name|The Videotape: Find Isambard Cruz|ct|CTPLOT_Ceres_Is_Isambard|desc|Follow Smiley's directions to Isambard's strange little store.

strTitle: Debrief with Smiley about the tape
strDesc:
You let out a pent up sigh. What to make of this? It could be anything. It could be nothing. Either way, there's no mystery how it grabbed the attention of a bunch of bored engineers.

You look at Smiley. Smiley looks at you.

"I have to admit," you tell him. "It's pretty cool."

"Yes!" he says. "I knew you'd say that. You have good taste."

strTitle: Say it's a load of rubbish
strDesc:
"What a load of crap," you say flatly. 

Smiley nods, his smile fading to a rare grimace. "Of course, sure," he says. "It's not as if ... no, you're right, of course."
You leave in search of Isambard Cruz.

This is definitely the address Smiley gave you, a hole in a ship wall with a sturdy door bolted on. Who exactly has he sent you to meet? You hit the buzzer. A moment's pause before a woman's voice replies: "Yes?" Surly, clipped, not entirely hostile. "Smiley sent me," you say, "if that's his name. I found a videotape. You've seen these before?" "Hold it up to the camera." You angle the 'Inhalants' label toward the tiny red bulb. Another moment as your offering is considered by the disembodied woman. The door unlocks with a loud ker-chack!. "Enter."
strTooltip: A red light glows, the recording signal of a bespoke security system.

strDesc:
Isambard Cruz puts you in mind of a schoolteacher you had on Arithmetic Disk 2. Tall, old, a bit too thin, a speaking voice so soft as to enchant and annoy you. She turns the video tape over in her hands like a fossil. "Yes," she mutters. "I know what this is."

Without breaking concentration, she beckons you closer. She indicates with her pinkie finger. "You know VHS, yes? Here, and here - fake studs. Not real, hah, reel." The homophones bounce off your skull. She looks up and scowls. "Fake."

"Why would someone make a fake video tape?" you ask. 

Cruz snorts. "Earth freaks, fetishists. They love car dice and I<3NY ballcap. They pay for it. Paid for it. Earth's the past. Market's dying." She sniffs again. "Good riddance." She was probably old enough to have come from Earth, you guess. She doesn't miss it.

"So what's on the tape?" You reach for it, but she turns and shuffles deeper into her shop. "I want to play it." You follow her, breathing in a mix of machine oil and incense. You trip over a cat, which hisses at you before returning to its idle animation. When you catch up to her she has the shell open on a workbench. She holds up a segment of tape to a single powerful lightbulb. 

"Is something," she mutters. "Old eyes can't see. You look, come." She bids you take the film. You hold it to your face, turning it this way and that. She continues to herself. "Real tape, magnetic." Chimes sound from the corner, turning in front of a desktop fan. The cat meows. "The fakes have film. Like what you see?"

The image resolves in a rush. A white-gold humanoid, the sarcophagus in miniature. The suggestion is so bracingly evil you lurch as if from an electric shock. Cruz laughs softly. "Yes," she says sadly. "It's never good."

She collects the offending strip of tape from you and shuffles over to another machine. She click-clacks on its oversized keypad. The machine, a gunmetal gray box with an LED readout canted toward her, whines to life.

She holds up one end of the length of tape to you, as if you have any idea of what she's doing and are keen to follow along, and inserts it into an aperture at the top of the machine. The machine's whine crescendos, and a deeper grinding thrums through the floor. Is she ... destroying it?

She senses your distress. "Digitisation," she says happily, stumbling a little over the English word. With one hand she feeds in the tape, the sound oscillating back and forth. "Cameras, inside," she says, running a pinkie along one edge. "And blades. Film, goes chop-chop-chop-chop poof! All the little pieces, tracked by little lasers. We get perfect copy at the end."

"You can't just photograph it?"

The machine screams. Isambard shakes her head. "That way is not perfect. This way it will live forever in the cloud."

It only takes a minute to digitise the rest. You hold a hand out to the Petware cat. She regards it dutifully. "How old is she?"

"Six months past warranty," says Isambard. "Like me!" And she laughs herself silly.

The machine sounds cease. Just as quickly she's handing you a data card, and inexorably chivvying you out the way you came in.

"Don't you want to see what's on it?" you ask.

"God in Heaven, no," she replies, and shuts the door in your face.
strSetPlotObjective: name|The Videotape: Return to Smiley|ct|CTPLOT_Ceres_Is_Smiley|desc|Doesn't this guy have a job?

strDesc:
Smiley flags you down eagerly. "Come in, come in!" he says. "The gang's all here." 

He ushers you inside.
strTooltip: He's still here. Doesn't he have a job?

strDesc:
The dorm is full of an electric heat; the AC is cracking along in double time trying to keep up with a dozen warm bodies. You're crowded the moment you enter by fans eager to see the tape. "Holy shit, it's the newbie! / Do you have it? / What's on it?"

Smiley cuts through the crowd and drags you centre stage. "Back off! This is the [us-custom-characterGenderCond|man|woman|hero] of the hour. Let'em breathe."

The simple act of passing off the drive with the video on it takes on an unavoidable degree of ceremony. A satisfied hush sweeps through the club as Smiley slots the drive into his PDA. He navigates to the file and hovers on its selection. "Before we begin," he says, "libations."

You'd noticed that most of the group have e-cigs or hand rolled cigarettes close by. Now they all have one or the other in hand, and are eagerly smoking away. A tall man you'd hazard a guess is Abacho hands you a little black weed pen. "Trust me," he says, "this is once in a lifetime."

"What's in it?" you ask.

"Marijuana," he says, and winks.

You shrug and take hit on the pen. You expect to cough, but it's incredibly smooth, and the taste is sweet, nothing like the harsh green bite of MJ.

You cough anyway as an experiment, look between the pen and Abacho. "There's no way in hell this is weed. What is it really?"

"It's home grown," he insists. "It tastes better, doesn't it?"

You flick the pen back. It oscillates over to him. "It should taste like weed, if that's what it is. Stay away from me, man."

"Thanks, but no," you say. "That's what the party actually's about? Just getting high? No offence, but that's like every third dorm on K-LEG."

Abacho tries to look offended while trying not to burn his fingers on the roach. "We're all about the kino. You'll see."

The player begins. Nothing, at first, happens.

Smiley looks at you, unaccountably nervous, as if you've messed something up.

"Come to me," says a voice. The room jumps. Someone yelps, and another laughs at their fright.

"Who said that?" says one of the Mollys, and everyone shushes her.

"Come to me," says the voice. Androgynous, toneless, soft but resonant in this small space. At the corners of the image, arcs of white appear. You're looking into the black sun as you drift away.

"Come to me," it says.

"Rule of threes," says someone knowingly. "Yeah, I'll be right there!" says another.

The player pauses. Everyone yells at Smiley, his hand on the PDA. He raises a hand for calm. "No more talking! This is a first watch! No talking!"

The room calms. Molly Liu looks as if she's seen a ghost. Abacho struggles to keep his eyes open as he hits the pen for the umpteenth time. Smiley presses play.

"- for many peoples, these were the first gods. And the greatest of the deities, the king of all gods, Jupiter." The footage is being filmed surreptitiously from a desk, looking down on an amphitheatre to a lecturer in mid-ramble. Cut: A garland, white flowers linked with gold lace, is laid upon a dark haired youth. An unseen voice asks a question, and the youth replies. Blocky yellow subtitles translate it from Russian, or a similar Slavic tongue. Subtitles: "How're you feeling?" / "I'm okay." The youth smiles. Her eyes are bright gold. Cut: "What about the Vestal Virgins? They were sacrificed." A student close by lowers his hand, looking smug. "They were killed for a crime. Capital punishment. Very common, still practised today. Human sacrifice is a colonial invention," says the lecturer, "libel by Conquistadors to justify the invasion. You can do anything to someone you believe is demonic." Cut: A low voice drones. The garlanded youth floats down a steel accessway, white tassels streaming behind her. Men and women in conventional pressure suits follow and precede her, some kind of honour guard. The suits are adorned with colourful patchwork heraldry, strong reds and blues. A second voice, then a third, joins the droning in perfect fifths. More voices begin a contrapuntal melody. The melody is full of vibrato, verging on quarter tones. It must be a folk tradition, though one you've not heard. They pass through a bulkhead into a wide cargo hold. The youth dives into it. The honour guard fans around her, singing. On the other side of the hold, the sarcophagus. Cut: The dialogue continues. "But wasn't human sacrifice witnessed by the colonists? How is it libel if it actually happened?" "The scholarship is shockingly poor on the subject." The lecturer is replaced by an upside down view of the documentarian's face, right up his nostrils. He's a young Xinhuan or Malaysian man, and he scratches his nose, bored. "I think it's more likely they witnessed cultural practices alien to them, which they misinterpreted in a way convenient to them." Cut: The singing has stopped, save for one voice, which carries the melody as the youth floats into the open sarcophagus. She climbs inside, a solemn expression on her face. The singer closes the lid. Surrounding the sarcophagus is a network of coiled tubing and steel cylinders. The honour guard gathers at a central console, all except the singer, who kneels at the side of the sarcophagus. Pneumatic hissing from the cylinders. The singer halts his song, and taps twice on the lid. A singular dull thud comes from inside. The singer flashes the thumbs up to those at the console. In unison, they break back into song. Once again, the playback pauses, cutting the singing short. The uproar from the club is even more venomous but once again Smiley calls for quiet, waving urgently. "Listen! Can you hear that?"

Far in the distance, a plaintive voice cries: "Zhou? Where are you? Zhou?" It's a cry well known on K-LEG. Less common, maybe, on the Flotilla. AyoSec are inbound. "It's a sweep!" The room explodes into chaos. A handful run for the door. Whether or not they're coming for this group, it's best not to stick around to find out. You've got maybe thirty seconds to act.

strTitle: Make a break for it with the crowd
strDesc:
Whatever's on that tape isn't worth tangling with the law. You bolt for the exit, reaching it just ahead of the others.

Seconds later, you're outside, into the passageway. You have to throw yourself to one side to avoid an old spacer hurtling toward you.

A steady human tide racing helter-skelter pulls you away from the main access routes.

You defer to the wisdom of crowds.

Flotilla is a maze, and not one you're familiar with. If anyone has a destination in mind, they don't stop to tell you. You join the mad scramble, pausing occasionally to listen out for the sounds of Ayosec behind you, and at one confusing juncture, in front of you.

The congealed ships echo with gunfire and screams. It's unusual for AyoSec to operate beyond their stomping grounds around Ganymed, but as the well-armed Flotillans know, not unprecedented. You can hear when Ayo hit a pocket of resistance: the fire tempo spikes and the timbre of answering munitions takes on a distinctly illegal tone.

After gaining some distance on the advancing corporate forces, the crowds slow down, and the tone shifts from panicked to wary. People form slower-moving knots, coordinating and keeping lookout and trying desperately to access the wireless mesh.

Trying to slip through the panicky human tide is difficult going. Nobody's prepared for some damn fool running into them, as you are. The next few minutes is kinetic chaos as you alternate between squeaking by on the periphery and shoulder-checking two, three people whenever you need to cross the passage.

The flow against you ceases without warning. Rounding a corner, you face an AyoSec compliance team.

Smiley's gone from his customary position at the PDA. You hit play, heedless of the confusion around you.

The singing returns in full force, a warm counterpoint to the impending threat. The timeline preview shows the honour guard milling around without change, so you track forward a couple of times, looking for anything that stands out. The singing cuts and chops sharply.

There! A flicker. You scrub back. The audio is overwhelmed with static, and in a heartbeat, the sarcophagus goes from inert to brighter than the sun, whiting out the screen.

"What the fuck!" says someone in the room, either following the video or unprepared for the blinding light, or at a burst of gunfire. 

"This is Ayotimiwa Security," says an amplified voice outside. "This is a routine zoning compliance sweep. Present your identity papers and residential licence. Show us empty hands or be shot on sight."

You scrub to the end of the video. The honour guard cheer, hug each other, weeping for joy.

The sarcophagus is open, and the youth is nowhere to be seen.

The Flotilla has been the victim of idiosyncratic retrofitting since day one. There's bound to be another way out.

Taking stock of the room, Smiley is nowhere to be found. There's a press at the door as several try to exit at once. Abacho stands nervously against one wall, by one of the interior doors. He waves at you.

You bound across the low common area, almost colliding with Molly Liu as she emerges from the kitchenette with a sawn-off flechette gun. You give her a wide berth. She cocks the gun, mouth set, and heads for the exit too.

You reach Abacho at speed, bouncing off the wall. He catches you. "In here, in here!" he says.

It's a bunkroom, where three others from the club are waiting nervously.

Two walls of the cramped bunkroom are inset bunks, stacked four high. The far wall is festooned in foldout storage blocks, all closed. One is covered by a "Hang In There!" poster, showing a muscly Petware cat doing pullups on an iron bar.

Abacho rips it down to reveal an exposed vent shaft. "There's a safehouse. Go one left, fifty metres. Two rights, then one left. Got that?" There's a harried chorus of assent. "Good enough. Get in!"

The remnants of the AV Club wedge themselves into the vent. When it's your turn, Abacho steps between you and the hole. "One moment. This is important."

He searches your eyes. Unbidden, you stare back into his. Is it your imagination, or are they tinged with flecks of gold?

He nods, satisfied. "I had to know. Smiley vouched for you, but he's gone. He might be a rat, I don't know. But you're good."

"Ayosec is coming for you?"

He shrugs. "It doesn't matter. Sooner or later, something was coming." He lays down on the floor, hands over his head. "Get out of here. I'm the legal resident. They might just let me live."

With one last look at the prostrated man, you climb into the vent.

Abacho produces the weed pen you rejected earlier.

"We have zero time here, so I'm going to be very clear. Smoke this, right now. Or take your chances outside."

Every ounce of confusion and outrage condenses into a single word: "What?!" But Abacho is unimpressed.

"Smoke it now," he repeats testily. "3, 2, 1, smoke."

It's slow going. The vent network is almost inhumanly tight, and everyone grows familiar with accidental kicks to the face. Abacho's directions are superfluous, as his route is also the only one you're able to fit through.

In the meantime, you have plenty to listen to. The metal underneath resonates with boots tromping, screams, and sporadic gunfire. Your fingers slip on the surface as your sweat forms a greasy layer across your upper body.

Everyone freezes as you crawl past a dorm room being invaded by Security. You watch the scene unfold through the a vent grille. The officers storm the room, round up the residents, and cable tie their hands. There's little you can do besides wait, desperately afraid to make a sound. One of the younger, sprier captives tries to make a break for it when he sees an opening, but a round catches him in the spine before he makes it to the door. Less-lethal or not, he stops moving.

Then there's a rigamarole of theatre as the individuals have their IDs scanned, which are invariably found wanting, and are packed into cubes aboard the skiff idling in the passageway.

After an indeterminate length of crawling, you hear a dreaded noise that wakes you from the monotony.

Down the length of shaft behind you, a horrible whining. "Wasps," you mutter, nonplussed. "Wasps!" you yell again to those ahead of you, and you push heavily on their boots.

"Wasps, wasps!" shout those in front, taking up the cry, and suddenly silence is forgotten, you're racing hand over hand as fast as you can.

There's little use. The first bogey zips past you, seeking the head of your formation. You catch a glimpse of it, an evil little bug with a needle-fine proboscis. The latest in AyoSec's compliance toolkit.

The air wing descends upon you, an uncountable number in the swarm. You writhe, desperately shucking off the needles burrowing into your clothes and skin. The first needle to find purchase slides into your left shoulder blade. A horrible pinprick of pain; an ocean of blissful numbing calm overwhelms your body. The wasp falls from your back, dead, its payload delivered.

In eerie unison the swarm moves past you, seeking their next victim, but it's a bad stick, too close to the bone. You can still move. Groggy, you watch as the woman in front of you is stung, and goes limp.

The simplicity of your objectives has you locked in. Each step arrives to you as a lucid, concrete action, activating a survival routine your mushy consciousness never fully knows. Push feet aside. Wriggle until parallel. Hook arm under arm. Use other arm to pull. Use pulling arm to try to prevent crash. Crash anyway. Recover, barely. Repeat.

Memory ceases recording. The body remains in motion. A kaleidoscope of vents and fans and bodies splits and reforms.

The blackwhite orb from Videotape 3 takes up residence inside your eyelids, surfing along novel circuitries of serotonin. "Come to me," it says. The girl goes inside the sarcophagus. Voices join in sweet harmony. "Come to me."

"I said I would," you mutter. You feel your hands waving, trying to swim. "You don't have to repeat it."

"I'll see you soon," it says.

"I can't move," you say. Your eyes are closed.

"You're strapped to the wall," says a man's voice, "because you're still asleep."

With effort, you open your eyes.

You're in a sleeping strap on the wall of a hard plastic blister. Half a dozen people are with you in the tiny space, trying to stick to its surfaces; to either side, sleepers are strapped against the wall - including the woman you saved. You rest your head. Your heart swells.

You pass in and out of sleep. The other occupants of the safehouse are less agitated each time you wake, and the sounds from the rest of Flotilla less distressing. In time, you regain most of your motor functions. Soon enough, you're able to leave the safehouse in ones and twos.

You leave with the woman you saved - Molly Oladele, whom the AV Club had dubbed Molly Two. You rejoin the flow of foot traffic on Flotilla. It's depressed, deflated; emergency crews are at work on every other bulkhead, and battered-looking people wander aimlessly or weep in the corridors.

The time comes for you to part ways, you to your ship, she to a shift on station. An uncomfortable frisson passes between you. "Thank you," she says at last, "for what you did."

You demur as best you can. She ignores your words. "I've been having dreams. All this will come to an end."

She looks in your eyes, suddenly intense. "Spend your final days wisely. Make them count."

You have to bite your tongue as she, having said this, leaves for work.

strTitle: Ask to hear Smiley's Extras commentary
strDesc:
Smiley eagerly runs the video back and begins pointing out every detail to his knowledge, along with a few guesses masquerading as knowledge.

"We've tried tracking down where we are, to start with," he says, gesturing to the asteroid and its starfield. "Molly 2 spent weeks trying to triangulate the co-ordinates from the constellations and the angle of the sun. I think it drove her a little bit mad."

"What did she learn?"

Smiley snorts. "That it was somewhere in the Belt," he says. "Fat lot of good that did us. We had better luck with the grapple rigs. They're rare enough that there's only a couple of Belter communities that use them, in a couple of asteroid groups, since their heyday in the colony rush. Of course, if it was filmed then, which we don't know, then we're back to square one."

"What will you do if you find it?" you ask. "Go there?"

Smiley laughs, but the mirth fades quickly. "Nah. We're stuck here."

Smiley skips through until the university advertisement. "Okay, now this, this is Voltaire University, right? On Luna. That's Earth up there," he says.

"There it is," you agree.

"So with this part, what's crazy is, there is no such ad, officially," he says. "I did the legwork myself. Kinda went nuts calling around everyone I could who'd answer a message on Luna, asking to dig through archives and so on. I watched a lot of ads, looking for this." Something in his tone tells you, it was hundreds and hundreds of hours of media.

"So it's a fake ad?"

Smiley chews some popcorn thoughtfully. "Dunno. There's a small holy war in the club over whether this part's AI or not. It's an offshoot from the main war over whether all the tapes are AI or not."

A total quagmire, then. You study the CEO's frozen smile, and compare it with Smiley's. Perhaps there's kinship there. "You seem to have an opinion on it," you say.

"Oh yeah," he says readily. "I know it's not AI, because it's not trying to sell me something."

He fast forwards again, throwing out a comment here and there, and holds it on the sarcophagus. You take a good minute and study it in closer detail, as close as the resolution and uneven lighting will allow. "Now," you say, "what's ... going on, here?" "That is the million dollar question," he says soberly. "We don't know." "That's all you have to say? You don't know?" His smile dims a little. "That's the long story short. The short story, um, medium, is that the sarcophagus comes up here, in #2, and again in #8. The numbers are meaningless." He corrects himself. "Not meaningless, but not chronological either." "What is it?" "A big gold human effigy," he says. "I don't know. They - the people in the videos - seem to revere it. They worship it. In the other video they put all kinds of science gizmos around it and talk to it or pray to it, but there's no audio. It's like a gnostic, new age, high tech religion. If only the Ancient Egyptians could see us now." "There must be a reason," you say. "People don't worship things for no reason." Smiley mulls over that idea. "I suspect," he says, "people worship what they're told to."

The crowd steadily funnels into a disused cargo bay on a mining ship once known as the Primary Consumer. The Flotilla community has set up a makeshift aid station. Displaced residents float to and fro, calling or texting or intensely questioning one another. An awkward contingent of Ayosec goons are here, too, temporarily on their best behaviour, while their lieutenants liaise with harried and haggard community leaders. You grab a patch of wall and make yourself scarce. The show is over, even if it's outstayed its welcome as particularly bad shows do. You listen to the churn of the rumour mill. Nobody knows what's going on, except that Ayo's strike has run out of steam, and they seem to be losing interest in the whole affair. With nothing to do but wait, you ruminate. The timing of the sweep seems far from coincidental. Was this about the videotape? Smiley's club? Could this be, even, about you? Ayotimiwa's bottom line would be impacted by this; a vast expense carried out for what are, as far as you can tell, intangible returns. Surely it's not to do with the contents of the tape, part of you insists. A glitchy soi-disant ARG can't be worth killing for ... unless it can. Does that possibility recontextualise the tapes? What part of them was important? Your thoughts chase themselves in circles, so that you barely notice when an Ayo drone scans your ID and instructs you to return to your ship of origin.

strTitle: Try to slip through Ayosec's lines
strDesc:
Doubling back, you move oblique to the danger, searching for an uncovered exit, a gap in the dragnet.

Unfortunately for you, AyoSec know this particular warren better than you do. Whenever you get on to a promising route, you wind up face to face with fast-setting foam barriers set from the other side, totally impenetrable with the time available to you. Reversing course, your options narrow, and narrow again, until eventually your luck runs out.

The men and women on the front line brace behind an row of interleaved ballistic glass shields. They themselves are kitted out in Testudo hardsuits, the helmets bristling with bugeyed imaging tech, and their snub-nosed weapons peek out of eyelets in the shield wall. Further down the passageway you glimpse the bulk of the skiff, the oddly boxy boarding craft Ayo uses for infantry support. A voice crackles over the loudspeaker, sharp and accustomed to command. "Advance!" A thin, reedy whistle sounds out, blown by someone safely behind the front line. The shields ripple, suit thrusters hiss. The wall advances slowly, inexorably, toward you.

You lay down sharply, hands behind your head. "Citizen!" you yell into the floor, spittle bouncing back into your face. "Azikiwe citizen!" "Advance," booms the officer's amplified voice again, somehow terse while also verging on bored. "Drop anyone moving." They open fire: a series of sharp cracks followed by the eerie whistle of subsonic rounds zipping by your head. Rough stippled gloves, and a boot to the head, transfer you behind the line as the shields float above you. "Subdue, restrain, verify," says the officer's voice. You're turned around to face your captors, slammed back against the wall in the process, your skull ringing like a bell. Once your ID is processed, you're fed head-first into a human storage cube, where you have plenty of time to think, and not a lot to do.

strSetPlotObjective: name|The Videotape|ct|TIsPlayer|desc|Lay low until all of this blows over.
strDesc:
An unknown amount of time passes in the cube. There's just enough space and ambient motion that you are constantly, literally, bouncing off the walls.

At the end of the unknown time period, which couldn't be more than half an hour, the viewing port slides up. An Ayo street Judge peers in. She reviews your case in twenty-three seconds flat. You're found noncompliant with eight of Ayotimiwa's core values in key growth areas of time management, interpersonal communication, and respect for authority. "What does that mean?" you ask. She taps the screen of her PDA, where your appointed HR rep is idling in a voice chat.

"Roughly, it means, wrong place, wrong time," says your HR rep, his audio icon jiggling with each word. "All told, you'll be out of pocket $523."

"Five hundred dollars?!"

"And twenty-three," he says smoothly. "If you want we can try and bargain them down, but as your representative, I'd advise you to take the rap and pick up some extra shifts."

You grit your teeth. It's difficult to bargain when you're crammed into a cube like a dehydrated mushroom. "Guilty as charged." The Judge nods, and the viewing port slides down.

After another four minutes, you're released to the tram station.

"Hell no," you say. "I'm not smoking your shit." He flicks it at you dismissively. It glances off your temple just hard enough to sting. "Have a good evening, officer." "I'm not a cop," you protest, aware it's falling on deaf ears. "I just don't want to smoke weed right now!" Abacho lays down, hands behind his head, preparing to be arrested. "It's not weed," he says. "But I think you know that." "I didn't know that!" He keeps his face to the floor, pointedly. "Then if I were you, I would start running."

Back in the common room, the party's over. The futons are scattered, popcorn floating through the air like confetti. 

The riot police outside sound awfully close. With no other avenue available, you go outside to meet them.

Where the hell did Smiley go? He was standing right there, not a moment ago.

"Smiley? Smiley!" you yell into the furor. It occurs to you that that was a forum handle. What was his real name? He introduced himself at one point.

You grab someone's shoulder in passing, knocking them off their axis. "What?!" they say. It's Xavier, the club's resident simulation theorist. 

"What happened to Smiley? Where'd he go?"

"Get the fuck off me!" says Xavier, righting himself, before he hurries after the rest.

Something bumps your shoulder: the light kiss of objects in space. It's Smiley's enormous glasses. You snag them on the rebound. Yep, it's the same pair, alright. Did they get knocked off?

Looking around, you spy another odd accoutrement, peeking out from underneath a futon. Something sleek, on bulbous fabric. You tug on one end.

The curio comes loose. It's a prosthetic bald cap, attached to a distinctive hairpiece with a receding hairline.

In either hand, you hold the two most recognisable features of the man you knew as Smiley.

The man is dead serious. You must smoke this drug or else. "Fine," you say, biting the word. "Fine! Give it." You inhale on the pen. One Tharsis City, Two Tharsis City, Three ... you glance at Abacho. He motions keep going. You glare at him, and keep inhaling. Eventually it is enough. You hand the pen back. "That wasn't weed," you say. Do the corners of your vision blur a little? No. "What is it?" Abacho shrugs. He stands aside from the vent shaft. "Left, two rights, left. Remember. Get going while there's time."
